1:
Calvin insists that anyone reflecting rightly on Isaac's birth must begin with the promise, since the text says not only that God had respect to Sarah but that he did as he had spoken. He finds a deliberate emphasis in the repetition, and notes that God delayed making Abraham a father until his body was nearly withered. Henry says the same in his own way, that long looked for comes at last, and that promised mercies come not at the time we set but at the time he sets, which is the best. Ellicott adds a smaller observation, that the promise in the earlier chapter was given by Elohim while the fulfilment here is credited to Jehovah, and Gill reads the visiting simply as mercy keeping its word, a reading Wesley states in Henry's own words, that Abraham and Sarah were both as good as dead and then the word of God took place.

Ellicott notices two irregularities in the naming, that the father names the child and does it at birth rather than at circumcision, and concludes no settled rule yet existed. Calvin removes the difficulty differently, that Abraham invented nothing but kept the name the angel had given, acting as a herald proclaiming what was committed to his trust. Henry makes it a lesson, that Abraham might have chosen a name of more pompous signification and did not, since human invention should yield to the plainness of divine institution. He draws four senses out of the name, the father's laughter of joy, the mother's of distrust, the mockery Isaac would endure, and the joy of all the saints.

On the circumcision Henry observes the symmetry, that since God kept time in performing the promise Abraham must keep time in obeying the precept, a bloody ordinance not to be deferred even for a darling. Calvin praises the same obedience as a setting aside of human affection, and turns it against his opponents, that nothing matters more in sacraments than taking God's bare word for the rule. He names the abuse, that God delivered two sacraments to the church and the papists boast of seven, as though men might forge promises of salvation and seal them with signs of their own imagining.

Sarah's laughter is read as joy rather than doubt, and Clarke compares the disciples who believed not for joy, taking the word for a pleasure that almost suspends the reason. Henry gathers three reflections, that God gives mercies to encourage joy in his service, that mercies long deferred are the more welcome, and that any mercy is doubled when friends rejoice. Calvin dismisses the rabbinic story that infants were brought for Sarah to suckle and disprove a rumour that the child was supposititious, since the plural means no more than that she called herself a nurse. Both he and Henry make her nursing an argument for mothers, Henry that a woman of quality with nurses at hand still did her duty, Calvin that to avoid the trouble without cause is to be half a mother.

Clarke turns the weaning into a philological excursion, deriving the English word from an Anglo-Saxon verb meaning to turn from one thing to another. He and Ellicott both canvass the age, Jerome reporting opinions of five years and twelve, the Maccabees suggesting three, and the Koran fixing two. Calvin asks why the feast fell here rather than at the birth or circumcision, rejects Augustine's reading that it teaches us to stop being children in understanding, and answers that the day is named because Ishmael's mocking came to light on it. He adds that the feast is recorded without reproach, since God does not forbid entertaining friends liberally at a birth, and Keil and Delitzsch supply the phrase that carries the story on, that the object of holy laughter was made the butt of unholy wit.
9:
What Ishmael did is not stated, and Clarke, after reporting that the Targums make it an idolatrous rite and others a ridicule of Sarah's age, closes the question with the remark that conjectures are as useless as they are endless. Ellicott fixes the limits from either side, dismissing the readings that charge gross wickedness, since Abraham would not then have found the expulsion so grievous, and equally the Septuagint's harmless playing, since Sarah's anger would then have been unjust. Calvin locates the offence in the word itself, noting that the participle applied to Ishmael and the name Isaac come from one root, so that both are sons of laughter in wholly different senses, the one bringing joy from the womb and the other setting out to destroy it. Henry adds the domestic aggravation, that a boy fourteen years the elder owed care to a child who was no match for him. Gill notes that Ishmael is nowhere named in the verse but only described as the son of Hagar the Egyptian, which he takes for a deliberate slight, while Wesley, following Henry, dates the four hundred years of Egyptian affliction from this very mockery.

How Paul could call this persecution is answered by Calvin with a question of his own, whether it was done with sword or violence, and the reply that the scorn of a virulent tongue does not injure the body but pierces the soul. Ellicott explains the provocation circumstantially, that a youth heir for fourteen years and now displaced could hardly keep his temper at a banquet held in his rival's honour. He goes further and blames the arrangement rather than the boy, that such jealousies are the inevitable fruit of polygamy, which makes a father's life wretched with the intrigues of women for their children. Henry reads it as older enmity still, that the seed of the serpent has a rooted quarrel with the seed of the woman, so the children of promise must expect to be mocked.

Sarah's demand strikes several of them as harsh, and Clarke softens it by translation, arguing that the verb means to divorce as well as to drive out, so that what she sought was a legal act barring Ishmael from the inheritance. Ellicott softens the other term, that the word rendered bondwoman properly means handmaid and is used elsewhere of a king's secondary wives, so the English unduly depresses Hagar's condition and with it the Jewish church in Paul's allegory. Calvin concedes that Sarah spoke more imperiously than became a wife whom Peter holds up as a pattern of subjection, and still maintains her tongue was governed by the Spirit, since Paul cites her words as an oracle. Henry takes the same view of the sentence, that though spoken in heat it stands as prophecy against all who have a place in the visible church without the new birth, since Ishmael might be Isaac's play-fellow and never his fellow-heir.

Henry analyses Abraham's distress in two parts, grief that Ishmael had given the provocation and grief that Sarah demanded so much, since correction might have served. Ellicott adds a third that the others miss, that Abraham thought the proposal not merely painful but unjust. Calvin is harder on him, holding that paternal affection made him try to confound a distinction God had drawn, and that God let his judgment fail him partly to humble him and partly to show every age that grace is dispensed by God's will alone. Keil and Delitzsch settle the phrase that resolves the matter, that in Isaac shall seed be called means neither that his descendants would take Isaac's name nor that they would be created, but that in Isaac alone would there be a posterity recognised as such.
12:
Clarke reads God's answer as vindicating Sarah's counsel while sparing Abraham's feelings, since the promise to Ishmael is renewed in the same breath. Ellicott renders the decisive phrase as saying that the seed which shall especially be accounted Abraham's and inherit the promises is the one sprung from Isaac. Calvin makes the point sharper, that God tells Abraham to obey his wife not because he approves her temper but because the work is his own, and that in such matters he inverts the accustomed order of nature on purpose. Before drawing out Paul's use of the story he enters a caution against the method itself, that Paul's allegory is no warrant for torturing every history into one, as Origen did, who by hunting everywhere for allegories corrupted the whole of Scripture while his imitators extracted smoke out of light.

Within those limits Calvin takes the two sons for the perpetual condition of the church, the faithful born of the incorruptible seed of the gospel and the hypocrites who feign what they are not and hold a place among the sons of God for a time. He presses the comparison into his own controversy, that as Ishmael was inflated with the vain title of the firstborn, so men who arrogate everything to themselves ridicule the faith of the simple. The boast of a long succession, he says, amounts to no more than Ishmael proclaiming himself the eldest, and a single clause disposes of it, that the sons of the handmaid shall not be eternal inheritors. His consolation for those who suffer such contempt is that every age has its Ishmaelites, and that those who hold the chief place in the church will not always remain within it.

On the promise made to Ishmael himself the sources differ in temper. Gill traces the nation to the Ishmaelites, the Saracens and the Turks, and refuses the Targum's rendering of them as a people of thieves, since a promise given for Abraham's comfort would hardly describe his son's seed as robbers. Ellicott observes drily that Hagar is never once acknowledged as Abraham's wife, though her child receives a noble promise for his father's sake. Wesley goes further than any of them in the other direction, that the casting out was not Ishmael's ruin and we cannot know it was his eternal ruin, since it is presumption to say that all who fall outside the external dispensation of the covenant are shut out from every mercy.

Henry admires the manner of the obedience more than the act, that it was speedy, following at daybreak upon a night's vision, and submissive, contrary to Abraham's own judgment and yet offered without a word of objection. Calvin measures the cost instead, that a man sending away his firstborn was tearing out his own bowels, and finds here the true test of faith, when the affections of nature, in themselves neither evil nor vicious, are resigned to the will of God. He also asks the question the narrative invites, why so slender a provision when the house was full of servants and beasts, and answers that Abraham may have kept them short on purpose so that they should not go far and he might still help them. Clarke and Ellicott jointly remove the appearance of cruelty by arithmetic, since Ishmael was fourteen at Isaac's birth and about seventeen at the weaning, so that the word rendered child implies nothing about age and the picture of a boy carried on his mother's shoulder is a mistake of the English.
15:
Ellicott tells the scene as narrative, a mother wandering and husbanding the water, the young life withering first, and at last the fainting body cast almost angrily under a shrub by a woman whose grief granted her no rest. Both he and Clarke explain why the boy failed first, Ellicott that a youth of seventeen in an age when men married at forty had not come to his strength, Clarke that the young bear fatigue worse and cannot endure thirst as their elders can. Clarke reads the act gently, that she put him under the shrub to screen him from the heat rather than abandoning him. Gill records the Jewish account that Hagar had turned back to the idols of Pharaoh's house and the water failed at once, and Wesley observes that not a word of Ishmael's is reported, only sighs that cried loud in the ears of mercy.

That God heard the boy and not the weeping mother is the difficulty Calvin takes up. He refuses the easy answer that the two were brought to repentance, seeing no sign of it, and concludes the cry was heard not for any faith in it but because God was mindful of what he had promised Abraham. He hears a reproof in the angel's question, that Hagar tormented herself instead of remembering a former deliverance in the same wilderness, and takes the words where he is to mean that a boy cast into solitude still has God near him. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both notice that it is the angel of Elohim here where it was the angel of Jehovah earlier, Ellicott explaining that Hagar was then within Abraham's family and is now outside it.

Whether the well was made for her or merely shown to her divides them. Gill allows that her eyes may have been held or swollen with weeping, or that the spring was created on the spot, and repeats the rabbinic notion that it was made at the world's beginning. Ellicott follows Abravanel in holding the well already existed and that God opened her eyes to some sign of it, trees or green growth, and Clarke agrees the words mean no more than that God directed her to water not far off. Calvin takes the same view and draws his lesson from it, that when God withdraws his care we are as far from help close at hand as if it lay at the ends of the earth, so we must ask not only for good things but for the prudence to see them, or we shall faint with closed eyes in the midst of fountains.

Ellicott explains the command to hold the lad as pointing to the future rather than the moment, and cites Jerome that a boy walking hand in hand with his mother was plainly no burden on her shoulder. Keil and Delitzsch place the wilderness of Paran, while Gill quotes a traveller's account of it as waterless and without man, beast, bird or grass, and at once observes that this can only be true of parts of it or Ishmael could not have lived there. Ellicott notes what the choice implies, that Ishmael sought neither Egypt nor a Canaanite town but the wandering life the Arabs keep still, though the Egyptian wife would strengthen the heathen strain in his descendants. Calvin turns even that marriage to account, that a wild man of the desert still submitted to his mother in taking a wife, which he thinks condemns Rome for overthrowing so plain a right of nature.
22:
Gill dates the visit not to Ishmael's marriage but to the weaning and the expulsion, and Henry reads the king's approach as the promise of a great name coming true, since a landless sojourner finds his friendship courted, God's favour being so visible that neighbours cannot help remarking it. Ellicott identifies both visitors as titles rather than names, Father-King for a Philistine ruler and mouth of all for his vizier and commander, and dates the visit well into the sojourn, when the earlier warmth had cooled over quarrelling herdsmen. He then turns the scene against Abraham, that a man now powerful enough for a king to seek alliance with looks the worse for having once abandoned Sarah and taken presents in compensation, while Abimelech behaves as generously as before. Calvin asks instead why so moderate a man should be suspected at all, and answers partly that the heathen take alarm without cause and partly that a household of servants the size of a small nation was reason enough.

Ellicott notes that the phrase about son and son's son is not the usual one but an idiom for kith and kin, met again in Job and Isaiah. Calvin explains the oath's clipped grammar, that to say if thou shalt lie is a Hebrew way of leaving the apodosis unspoken, the sense being that God is called to sit as judge and avenger of perjury. Clarke describes the accompanying rite of slaying a beast and passing between the pieces, and finds in Abimelech's appeal to past kindness the root of the ancient rule of like for like. Both Henry and Calvin approve the readiness with which Abraham swore, Calvin that nothing is more absurd than for the sons of God to look morose when something just is asked of them, and Henry that religion ought not to make men sour to all company.

The well is the real business, and Clarke explains why, that in those countries water was scarce and a well cost much time and labour to find. Calvin wonders why Abraham had not sought redress earlier from so humane a king, suggests he may have known the seizure happened through the king's own excessive forbearance, and praises his patience under an injury which was as good as an attempt upon his life. Ellicott reconstructs the diplomacy, that the herdsmen's theft had chilled the friendship, that Abimelech came to find the cause, and that with Oriental indirectness he made no complaint but hinted at his own past kindness until Abraham took the meaning and spoke. Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke both exonerate the king, who had not heard of the act until that day and ordered the well restored as a matter of course.

Clarke suggests the sheep and oxen were the sacrifices for the occasion, furnished by Abraham and handed to Abimelech to offer as a mark of honour. Calvin reads them differently, as tribute rather than a present between equals, since among the Hebrews the offering of gifts is what the Latins called paying tax and what we call doing homage. He finds Abraham's modesty the more praiseworthy for being unprompted, since he did not wait for the king to extort anything but offered of his own accord what he thought due to another man's office. That raises the question whether a man to whom God had promised the land could lawfully acknowledge another as its lord, and Calvin answers that the time of possession had not come, so that Abraham was lord in expectation only and a pilgrim in fact.
28:
Ellicott explains the seven lambs from the language, that the Hebrew verb for swearing means to be sevened, so an oath was literally a thing confirmed by seven. He is unsure whether Abimelech's question shows the rite was strange to Philistines or is merely the courtesy that required him to ask. Calvin sees the practical necessity, that a stranger might have been challenged for digging a well at all, so the gift secured the king's authority behind the act. He rejects the suggestion that the lambs were coins struck in that shape, since sheep and oxen have just been named, while Clarke reads them as the price of the well and the witness of Abraham's title.

The name of the place divides on whether it means the well of the oath or the well of seven. Clarke and Wesley take the oath, and Calvin with them, admitting the vowels do not answer exactly but observing that proper names are not nicely governed by grammar. Ellicott takes the seven with a covert allusion to the oath, and adds what none of the others could, that Robinson found the site with the name still living. He describes two masonry-lined wells reaching never-failing springs, with stone troughs round them and the parapet of the larger worn into deep grooves by the ropes.

What Abraham planted is a tamarisk rather than a grove, and both Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch say so, Ellicott recalling the tree under which Saul held court and another beneath which his bones were laid. Keil and Delitzsch make the choice significant, that a long-lived tree of hard wood and evergreen leaves was a fit type of the enduring grace of the covenant God. Gill reports the rabbinic guesses at its use and inclines to an oratory with an altar in the midst, adding that the later heathen abuse of groves may have begun so. Calvin notices what the planting implies, that a man who had shifted his tent for sixty years is never before said to have set a single shrub in the ground.

Clarke turns the word into a long excursion on sacred trees among the nations, from the asylum Romulus opened between two oak groves to the oracle at Dodona and the Druids named from the oak. He quotes Pliny on the cutting of the mistletoe with a golden hook, and cannot read it without thinking of one who had no father on earth, was given to heal all our ills, and after being cut off was wrapped in fine linen. On the act of worship he adopts Shuckford's objection that the Authorised Version renders the phrase very erroneously, since the Hebrew means to invoke in the name rather than to call upon it. He then argues that the word for everlasting can bear no limited sense here, and warns that anyone who softens it to shorten punishment must soften it equally for the blessed.

Ellicott traces a progression instead, that Abraham had claimed God as supreme and then received him as almighty, and now names him eternal. A man growing in holiness, he concludes, grew also in knowledge of the manifold nature of God, which is why the Hebrews said not El but Elohim, the plural gathering every attribute into one. Keil and Delitzsch tie the title to the covenant, and Calvin hears in it a disclaimer, that Abraham would not have it thought his confidence rested on an earthly king. Henry makes the closing point practical, that Abraham kept not a private practice but an open profession his neighbours could join, and that good men should propagate their goodness.
